metadata_extension.subtitle: China’s tariffs on U.S. commodities? A huge impact. Especially on bilateral trade. But also on global U.S. exports of soybeans. China’s tariffs on U.S. manufactures? By comparison, a relative modest impact.

summary.central_question: Why have China's retaliatory tariffs hit U.S. commodity exports hard but had little visible effect on U.S. manufacturing exports to China?
summary.main_thesis: China's retaliation has mainly hurt U.S. commodity exports, has been largely ineffective against manufactures, and falls in bilateral trade should not be read as falls in total trade or output.

content.text: Why have China's retaliatory tariffs hit U.S. commodity exports hard but had little visible effect on U.S. manufacturing exports to China?
content.reason: A policy's effect differs across sectors, so aggregate outcomes need sector-level explanation.

content.text: The author expected China's tariffs to cause a much larger fall in U.S. manufacturing exports than has occurred.
content.reason: When the data contradict your expectation, say so and revise the expectation.

passages.source_excerpt: And another (on manufactures) has had a more modest impact than expected.

content.text: U.S. commodity exports to China fell more than 60 percent, while manufacturing exports show no clear break at the tariff date.
content.reason: Compare the indexed series of tariffed sectors to see where the policy actually bit.

passages.source_excerpt: exports are down over 60 percent, and the fall isn’t over

content.text: Bown's work shows China tariffed 55 percent of U.S. exports, raising the average tariff from 8 to 18 percent and covering a decent share of manufactures.
content.reason: A tariff covering a large share of trade should leave a visible mark after enough time.

passages.source_excerpt: China, per Chad Bown of the Peterson Institute, has only put tariffs on 55 percent of U.S. goods exports

reasons: links: `E7` supports `P3` joins L2→L1, which no hand-drawn supports link does

content.text: U.S. manufacturing exports to China fell somewhat more than euro-area exports last fall, showing some tariff effect.
content.reason: A comparable untariffed exporter serves as a control for common demand shocks.

passages.source_excerpt: There was a bigger drop off in American exports to China than in European exports to China last fall

content.text: Part of the U.S. underperformance relative to Europe could reflect the dollar's strength rather than tariffs.
content.reason: Exchange-rate moves shift relative export performance independently of tariffs.

passages.source_excerpt: though not one so big that it could not be, in part, a function of the dollar’s strength relative to the euro

content.text: China has held back on some sectors, such as autos, to keep retaliation targets in reserve.
content.reason: A retaliator keeps leverage by not using all its threats at once.

passages.source_excerpt: China has exercised a bit of restraint, and held back on really restricting trade in some sectors to make sure it has targets to retaliate against

content.text: China lacks good manufacturing targets because many U.S. imports have no substitute or feed China's own exports, so tariffs on them would hurt China.
content.reason: Tariffs on essential or input goods mostly tax the importing country itself.

passages.source_excerpt: China lacks good targets, as the bulk of its manufactured imports from the United States are in sectors where there isn’t (for now) a domestic Chinese alternative

content.text: Earlier Chinese tariffs and indigenous-production policies had already cut U.S. construction equipment exports, from about $2 billion in 2012 to $0.6-0.8 billion.
content.reason: A market already lost cannot be squeezed further by new tariffs.

passages.source_excerpt: U.S. exports of construction equipment to China are less than half their 2011-12 levels even before the trade war started.

content.text: Commentators who think China can retaliate against U.S. construction and telecom equipment hold an out-of-date view, since the U.S. runs deficits with China in those sectors.
content.reason: In a sector where you are a net exporter, an exchange of tariffs costs you more.

passages.source_excerpt: it is common to argue that China might retaliate against U.S. construction equipment exports, and against U.S. switching equipment.

content.text: Studies find high trade elasticities to tariffs, which would predict the collapse in soybean trade.
content.reason: High price elasticity means a large tariff can eliminate bilateral trade.

passages.source_excerpt: With an elasticity of 4, a 25 percent tariff would be expected to zero out trade.

content.text: The soybean collapse may instead reflect state importers being directed not to buy U.S. beans.
content.reason: Where state firms dominate imports, administrative direction can replace price signals.

passages.source_excerpt: But it is also consistent with a world where China’s state importing companies were told not to buy American.

reasons: links: `P1` undercut_by `R2` joins L1→L6, which no hand-drawn undercut_by link does

content.text: Soybean exports went to near zero and farmers could not redirect sales, so total U.S. soy exports and prices fell.
content.reason: When one buyer dominates a market, losing it cannot easily be offset elsewhere.

passages.source_excerpt: The reduction in China’s purchases of soybeans clearly hurt American farmers who weren’t able to make up for the fall in Chinese demand

content.text: Oil exports to China fell near zero but overall U.S. oil exports and Permian pipeline investment were unaffected.
content.reason: Compare bilateral and total exports to separate diversion from destruction.

passages.source_excerpt: The tariffs diverted bilateral trade in oil away from China without impacting overall trade.

content.text: For fungible commodities with deep global markets, tariffs reroute trade rather than reduce it.
content.reason: Homogeneous goods with many buyers are easily redirected when one market closes.

passages.source_excerpt: That’s more or less what one would expect in a true commodity where it isn’t that hard to find alternatives to the Chinese market.

content.text: U.S. auto exports to China fell in late 2018 and rebounded when China lifted the extra tariffs; Alabama and South Carolina exports fell.
content.reason: Trade that moves in step with tariff changes points to a causal effect.

passages.source_excerpt: China’s tariff on autos did have an impact last summer and fall.

content.text: Automakers offset lost China sales by shifting SUV output to rising U.S. demand, so U.S. production plans were largely unchanged.
content.reason: Producers can absorb a lost export market if domestic demand for the same product is growing.

passages.source_excerpt: it is possible that Mercedes and BMW were effectively able to offset their reduced exports to China by producing more for the U.S. market.

content.text: Trade-by-state data for Alabama and South Carolina are a good proxy for BMW and Mercedes SUV exports to China.
content.reason: Regional trade data can stand in for firm-level flows when a few plants dominate a state's exports.

content.text: Auto exports to China would probably have fallen anyway as German firms localize production in China, which makes the tariff effect hard to isolate.
content.reason: Structural trends can mask or mimic a policy's effect.

passages.source_excerpt: The counterfactual here is hard.

content.text: Across soy, oil and autos, tariffs cut bilateral trade, but only in soy did they cause real economic and political damage.
content.reason: The harm from losing a market depends on how easily output can be redirected.

passages.source_excerpt: In all three cases, China’s tariffs reduced bilateral trade. But so far, China’s retaliation only looks to have been far more effective

content.text: China's retaliation has mainly hurt U.S. commodity exports, has been largely ineffective against manufactures, and falls in bilateral trade should not be read as falls in total trade or output.
content.reason: Bilateral trade shocks matter only to the extent that other markets cannot absorb the diverted goods.

passages.source_excerpt: Don’t equate changes in bilateral trade with changes in overall trade, or changes in total output. A lot depends on the sector.

content.text: Manufactures are defined as NAICS 300s and commodities as the 100s and 200s, without separating tariffed from untariffed goods.
content.reason: Broad aggregates that mix affected and unaffected goods dilute a measured policy effect.

passages.source_excerpt: Manufacturing exports come from the NAICs data, using all exports in the 300s.

reasons: passages: `SCP`: the team's passage linker anchors it to p43 (shared: naics), which the box does not cite

content.text: The modest implied manufacturing elasticity may be understated because untariffed goods were not separated out.
content.reason: Estimates from aggregates are limited by what the aggregation includes.

passages.source_excerpt: but I haven’t tried to disaggregate manufactures into those actually tariffed by China and those that have escaped so far

content.text: The full economic impact of China's retaliation remains an open question.
content.reason: Effects still unfolding in the data cannot yet be judged in full.

passages.source_excerpt: the debate on the overall impact of China’s retaliation on the U.S. economy is sure to continue
